newsitem.title: USA: Serbia says will not use force on protesters - U.S.
newsitem.headline: Serbia says will not use force on protesters - U.S.

text.p: Serbia has told the United States it will not use force to put down anti-government protests, the State Department said on Wednesday.

At a "very tough" meeting in London with Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic "made a promise that the Serbian government would not use force to disrupt these demonstrations," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
In response, Talbott told Milutinovic "we would judge the Serbian government based on its actions, not on these promises," the spokesman said.

Opposition and student supporters have shaken Yugoslavia's government and raised doubts about the future of President Slobodan Milosevic's rule by holding 17 days of demonstrations in protest at the outcome of local elections.

The United States, which has viewed Milosevic as central to its peacemaking efforts in Bosnia, was slow to express public support for the protesters and criticism of Milosevic's moves to rein them in. But this has changed in recent days.

On Wednesday, the administration moved to undercut Belgrade's shutdown of independent Radio B-92 by having the U.S. government's Voice of America broadcast reports from the radio's correspondents into Serbia.
VOA said it was expanding its medium- and short-wave Serbian-language transmissions from two to two-and-a-half hours daily to accommodate reports by B-92 journalists and interviews with them.
Serbian authorities closed down B-92 on Tuesday as protests continued in Belgrade over what opposition parties said was massive fraud by the ruling socialists in local elections last month.
The United States condemned the radio shutdown as "a transparent effort to keep the Serbian public in the dark."

"The Serbian people, listening to Voice of America, will be able to hear free and unfettered criticism of the Serbian government, a fair and honest account of what's happening on the streets of Serbia," Burns said.
"We think this is the least we can do for the people of Serbia who are being denied free access to information."
VOA, the international radio service of the U.S. Information Agency, broadcasts in 52 languages and claims 86 million listeners per week worldwide.

The adminstration also intensified its direct warnings to Milosevic, with Burns saying the Serbian leader "will not have our support if he continues his efforts to try to extinguish the flame of democracy that those protesters are carrying in the streets of Belgrade."
"Let me just be very clear about the position of the United States. The United States is taking the side of democracy with Serbia," Burns said.
He said "Milosovic probably needs us at this point more than we need him."

The White House and the State Department, in separate statements, commended the opposition for the peacefulness of its demonstrations and warned that "any crackdown by the Serbian government will provoke a harsh reaction from the international community resulting in Serbia's further isolation" from the international community.

Burns refused to say how Washington might react if Serbia tried forcefully to crush the protests. He talked only about taking "whatever steps we deem necessary to express our displeasure with future actions of the Serbian government."

Despite its condemnation of Milosevic's actions, the United States has stopped short of seeking to re-impose the full trade sanctions against Belgrade that the United Nations removed last year. U.S. officials have said Russia and possibly other nations would block such a move.

Instead Washington wants to maintain an "outer wall" of American sanctions that denies Serbia access to money from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, as well as membership in the United Nations and other organisations.

Earlier in the day in London, the United States and Western allies made a strong attack on Serbia during an international conference to review the peace process 12 months after the Dayton accord that ended 43 months of war in Bosnia.
